title: Spectrophotometry and Beer–Lambert (AP; colorimetry for A-level); Balanced equations and reacting masses
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AM12#t2 term and clue written for the game; AM07#t4 term and clue written for the game; AM12#t1 term and clue written for the game; AM07#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM07#N.4b, AM12#N.7, AM07#N.6b, AM12#N.9b, AM07#N.9, AM12#N.12a, AM07#N.12b, AM07#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Blank
items.clue: A cuvette of solvent alone, used to zero the instrument first.

items.label: Precipitate
items.clue: A solid formed when two solutions react, e.g. AgCl from Ag⁺ and Cl⁻.

items.label: Absorbance
items.clue: A reading with no units that shows how much light a sample takes in.

items.label: State symbols
items.clue: The labels (s), (l), (g) and (aq) written after each species in an equation.

questions.stem: A student writes the equation Cu(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ag(s) to represent the reaction of copper metal with aqueous silver ions. Which statement about the student's equation is correct?

options.text: It is not balanced, because the total charge differs on the two sides
It is balanced, because each side has one copper atom and one silver atom
It is balanced, because each side contains the same number of particles, two
It is not balanced, because Ag⁺ must be written as Ag₂²⁺ to match the charge on Cu²⁺

questions.explanation: Atoms match, but charge is 1+ on the left and 2+ on the right. Balanced: Cu(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s).

questions.stem: A cuvette with a path length of 0.500 cm holds 3.00 mL of a 2.00 × 10⁻⁵ M solution of a dye. At the dye's wavelength of maximum absorbance, the absorbance of the solution is 0.300. What is the molar absorptivity of the dye at this wavelength?
questions.explanation: ε = A ÷ (bc) = 0.300 ÷ (0.500 cm × 2.00 × 10⁻⁵ M) = 3.00 × 10⁴ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹. The 3.00 mL plays no part.

questions.stem: When aqueous solutions of lead(II) nitrate, Pb(NO₃)₂, and potassium iodide, KI, are mixed, a yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide, PbI₂, forms. Which of the following is the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction?
questions.explanation: Only the ions that form the precipitate. 1 Pb and 2 I each side; charge 0 each side.

questions.stem: The absorbance of a solution of a dye, measured at its wavelength of maximum absorbance in a 1.00 cm cuvette, is 0.90. A student mixes 20.0 mL of this solution with 10.0 mL of distilled water. Assuming that the volumes are additive, what is the absorbance of the diluted solution, measured in the same way?
questions.explanation: A ∝ c at fixed b and wavelength. c falls to 20.0/30.0 of its value, so A = 0.90 × 2/3 = 0.60.

questions.stem: A student is drawing a particulate representation of the reaction represented by the equation 2 Al(s) + 3 Cl₂(g) → 2 AlCl₃(s). The student's "before" box contains 6 Cl₂ molecules. How many Al atoms should the "before" box contain, and how many AlCl₃ formula units should the "after" box contain, if no reactant is to be left over?
questions.explanation: 6 Cl₂ is twice the 3 Cl₂ in the equation, so twice 2 Al and twice 2 AlCl₃. Check: 12 Cl before and after.

questions.stem: A green solution of nickel(II) ions is taken from a lab waste container. Its absorbance is measured under the same conditions as these nickel(II) standards. Standards (M : A): 0.050 : 0.16 · 0.100 : 0.32 · 0.150 : 0.48 · 0.200 : 0.64. The sample gives A = 0.40. What is its nickel(II) concentration, in M?
questions.explanation: The points lie on a straight line through the origin: A = 3.2 × c. So c = 0.40 ÷ 3.2 = 0.125. Reading across from A = 0.40 to the line gives the same value.

questions.stem: Excess AgNO₃(aq) is added to 25.0 mL of 0.100 M CaCl₂(aq), and all of the chloride ions precipitate as AgCl(s) (molar mass 143.32 g/mol). What mass of AgCl(s) forms?
A strip of magnesium burns brightly in air and leaves white magnesium oxide: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). What mass of MgO forms from 2.43 g of Mg? (Molar masses: Mg 24.31 g/mol, MgO 40.30 g/mol)
